title: Message Submission
summary: Describes a way for mail clients to submit messages to a server as a distinct step from relaying, and what a submission server should do. This separates sending from relaying and makes policies easier to enforce. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 4409.

plainLanguage.summary: When you drop a letter in a mailbox, it is handled differently from mail passed between post offices. This describes the special entry point for letters from users.

questions: how does mail submission differ from relay
what is a message submission agent
subtitle: Why email clients should hand new messages to a dedicated submission server on port 587, and what that server should do.

tldr.problem: SMTP was designed to transfer finished messages, yet mail clients also use it to introduce new, possibly incomplete, messages, and fixing them downstream causes harm.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves port 587 for message submission and defines a Message Submission Agent (MSA) with mandatory, recommended and optional actions, reply codes and permitted message modifications.
tldr.outcome: Separating submission from relay makes security policy and spam control simpler. This Proposed Standard has been obsoleted by RFC 4409.

today: RFC 2476 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4409, so that document is the one to read for message submission now.

sections.title: Submission Versus Transfer
sections.content:
SMTP was defined as a message transfer protocol: a way to route and deliver finished messages. Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) are not supposed to alter message text, apart from adding headers such as Received and Return-Path. But SMTP is now widely used for message submission too, where a Message User Agent (MUA) introduces a new message to the MTA network. The process that accepts these is the Message Submission Agent (MSA).

Submitted messages may be unfinished, for example lacking a proper Date header or using domains that are not fully qualified. Completing them downstream in MTAs has been shown to cause harm. Splitting submission from transfer makes it easier to apply security policy and block unauthorized relaying and bulk mail, support authenticated and off-site submission, keep relay and submission code separate, and detect client configuration problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Dropping a new letter into a mailbox is not the same job as a post office forwarding sacks of mail. This RFC gives the first job its own door.

sections.title: Port 587, Rejection and Authorization
sections.content:
Port 587 is reserved for message submission, and anything received on it is defined to be a submission. The protocol is ESMTP with extra restrictions. A site may instead use port 25 for submission by designating some hosts as MSAs and others as MTAs.

If an MSA cannot determine a return path for the submitting user, it SHOULD reject the message immediately with a 550 reply to MAIL FROM. A null return path (MAIL FROM:<>) MUST be accepted. For other problems the MSA MAY accept the message and send a bounce later, but immediate rejection is preferred because it gives the user direct feedback.

Authorization methods named include authenticated SMTP, IP address restrictions, secure IP and a prior POP authentication. The RFC notes that IP restrictions are widely used but cannot handle travellers and can be spoofed, and that the POP-first method burdens clients and servers and leaves a window for impersonation.
sections.plainLanguage: The special mailbox sits at door number 587. If the post office cannot tell who sent a letter, it hands it straight back instead of passing it on.

sections.title: What the MSA Must, Should and May Do
sections.content:
An MSA MUST ensure all domains in the envelope are fully qualified, and rejects improper ones with reply code 554. If it examines or alters the message text, it must do the same for address header fields. Local conventions that expand single-level domains SHOULD reject, not expand, incomplete multi-level domains.

An MSA SHOULD reject illegal address syntax (reply 501 for a bad MAIL FROM or RCPT TO) and SHOULD log errors, especially apparent client misconfigurations.

An MSA MAY refuse a sender with insufficient submission rights (550 with 5.7.1), refuse an unauthenticated session (530), refuse recipients that conflict with the user's permissions, and check message data against syntax, permissions or site policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The submission desk must make sure every address is complete, should send back letters with nonsense addresses, and may also check that you are allowed to send.

sections.title: SMTP Extensions and Message Modifications
sections.content:
The RFC lists which SMTP extensions apply on the submission port. Pipelining, Error Codes, Extended Codes, DSN and 8-bit MIME are SHOULD. Size, Checkpoint and Binary are MAY. ETRN and the 521 reply code are MUST NOT. Future extensions should state whether they are valid on the submission port.

Sites MAY modify submissions to meet standards and site policy, but the paramount rule is to limit changes to specific problems with clear solutions. Permitted changes include adding or replacing Sender, Date and Message-ID, transfer encoding, signing, encrypting, resolving aliases and rewriting addresses by specific local configuration. Data-independent rewriting rules, such as always deleting the first element of a domain, would be very dangerous. Unconditionally resolving aliases could lose useful information.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk may fix small mistakes on a letter, like a missing date, but should only fix what it is sure about, because a wrong guess breaks the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Keeping submission and relay apart lets a site apply different policies to each, including extra security for one or both, in a way that is simpler technically and administratively. That makes it more likely policy is applied correctly, and it helps track and prevent unsolicited bulk email.

For example, a site can require authentication at the MSA and have its MTA reject all RCPT TO for non-local users. A site that requires no form of authorization for submissions allows open use of its resources and name, and bulk email can be injected through it.
sections.plainLanguage: If the special mailbox lets anyone post anything without checking, bad people can use your name to send junk. Checking who is posting stops that.

items.label: General rejection
items.desc: Improper MAIL FROM, RCPT TO or DATA; with 5.6.0 if no code is more specific.

items.label: Bad address syntax
items.desc: Detectably improper address in MAIL FROM or RCPT TO.

items.label: Not allowed
items.desc: Insufficient submission rights, or recipient inconsistent with user permissions.

items.label: Site policy
items.desc: Message appears to violate site policy.

items.label: Bad domain or address
items.desc: Used after end-of-data with 554 for invalid addresses in the header.
